items.t: Glimpse wants to give hardware companies an X-ray view of every critical part
items.d: Called Explore, Glimpse's new image processing software lets hardware makers speed up quality control checks using CT scanners.
items.fullText: Recalls are no joke. Take the one that sidelined every Chevy Bolt made between 2017 and 2022: A problem at an LG battery factory caused some parts inside the cells to be installed improperly, which ultimately cost LG $1.9 billion . Pretty much every major manufacturer has to deal with recalls. In the EV space alone, Volkswagen, Stellantis, Hyundai, Toyota, and others have all suffered through them. “The majority of those major quality issues could have been caught with CT scanning. And the reason why they weren’t is because it’s way too slow to do any kind of statistical sampling,” Eric Moch, co-founder and CEO of Glimpse , told TechCrunch. To help companies find more defects, Glimpse has developed a way for battery manufacturers to inspect cells 10 to 30 times faster by significantly boosting throughput on their existing CT scanners. Using Glimpse’s software, manufacturers could scan tens of thousands of cells per day, up from the current handful, Moch said. A customer “super scanner” that Glimpse is developing with partners could complete a scan in a second or two, he added. Batteries aren’t the only parts to suffer from costly defects, of course, so Glimpse is launching a new product, the company exclusively told TechCrunch. Called Explore, the product will let customers in industries such as aerospace, automotive, electronics, and medical devices use the startup’s image processing software to speed up quality control checks using CT scanners in their labs and development environments. Glimpse currently has over 100 customers, such as Anker, Lucid, and the U.S. Navy, and currently generates revenue in the “mid seven-figure” range, Moch said. Customers include both buyers and sellers of batteries. To wring more speed out of traditionally slow CT scanners, the startup has written its own image processing pipeline, which compresses scans and cleans them up. items.fullText: EXCLUSIVE Artificial intelligence Artificial intelligence Global tech policymakers agree to embrace AI in science A joint statement issued by the U.S. and 15 other countries touts the technology’s potential to accelerate scientific progress. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room of the White House on Tuesday during a lunch meeting with top executives of AI firms as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, left, and Elon Musk listen. Jacquelyn Martin / AP Share Add NBC News to Google Oct. 3, 2026, 9:00 AM EDT By Jared Perlo The United States on Sunday will release a joint statement with 15 other countries describing a shared vision for a “golden age of science” that embraces the potential of artificial intelligence. The announcement is expected in Kyoto, Japan, at this year’s Science and Technology in Society Forum, an annual gathering of experts and policymakers that began in 2004. The statement, titled the “Kyoto Vision for a Golden Age of Science,” begins by recognizing science and technology’s benefits to society then goes on to encourage research that integrates artificial intelligence. (The statement calls it “super intelligence,” given President Donald Trump’s recent executive order renaming the technology.) “Super Intelligence and new ways of organizing research are opening entirely new frontiers of discovery,” reads the statement, which was seen by NBC News. “We recognize the opportunity to take advantage of these changes.” Michael Kratsios, head of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy, spearheaded the vision statement, which also says the participating countries welcome the “growing field of metascience,” a term that describes the study of the scientific process itself. Tech ministers from Japan, Korea, the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates were among the representatives from other countries that endorsed the statement. items.fullText: Artificial intelligence Senate Democrats block Husted-led bill on data centers, calling it ‘toothless’ The bill aims to prevent data centers from spiking local utility costs. Republicans accused Democrats of playing political games, noting the bill passed the House 417-3. Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images file Share Add NBC News to Google Sept. 30, 2026, 1:41 PM EDT By Sahil Kapur WASHINGTON — Senate Democrats blocked legislation Wednesday aimed at protecting consumers from paying higher prices when new data centers are built in their communities. The vote was 57-43, short of the 60 needed to break a filibuster. The Ratepayer Protection Act , which passed the House by a vote of 417-3 two weeks ago, would set a federal standard on the issue. It would also instruct state public utility commissions to find ways to make developers of data centers that use huge amounts of energy cover their own costs of water and electricity to consumers. The Senate version is led by appointed Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who’s locked in a competitive battle as he seeks his first full Senate term. He is facing heat at home from Democratic rival Sherrod Brown, a former senator who has branded him “the face of data centers” for promoting developments when he was lieutenant governor. “I heard they said they wanted lower electricity prices,” Husted said of Democrats on Tuesday. “All they have to do is not block it, vote for it, and it will be on the president’s desk, and we will have a bipartisan win.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said the bill would be merely “optional” for states and wouldn’t achieve much beyond partisan messaging for Republicans. “Plain and simple, the Ratepayer Protection Act is a fraud,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “It does not require any protections at all. While Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, Republicans are offering a toothless messaging bill.

items.fullText: 판타지의 경계를 확장하다: 삼성 스페이셜 사이니지가 도쿄게임쇼 2026에서 펼치는 캐릭터 IP와 리테일의 미래 2026/09/23 AI 요약 새로운 뉴스룸 AI 기능을 살펴보세요! 닫기 --> AUDIO Play Download 공유 레이어 열기 인쇄하기 9월 17일부터 20일까지 일본 지바현 마쿠하리 멧세(Makuhari Messe)에서 열린 도쿄게임쇼 2026(Tokyo Game Show 2026, TGS). 글로벌 게임 기업 엔씨 부스는 게임 속 캐릭터를 눈앞에서 만나는 듯한 경험을 하려는 관람객들의 발길이 이어졌다. 그 중심에는 게임의 세계관을 화면 밖으로 확장한 삼성전자의 무안경 3D 디스플레이 ‘스페이셜 사이니지(Spatial Signage)’가 있었다. 이번 행사에서 엔씨가 선보인 ‘아스트라에 오라티오(Astrae Oratio)’는 마법이 일상에 스며든 판타지 세계를 배경으로 한 신전기 서브컬처 RPG다. 삼성 스페이셜 사이니지는 독자적인 ‘3D 플레이트(3D Plate)’ 기술을 적용해 별도의 3D 안경 없이도 콘텐츠에 생생한 입체감을 선사하며, 게임 속 캐릭터와 세계관을 오프라인 전시 공간으로 확장했다. 팬덤 경험 확장… 캐릭터와의 만남을 현실 공간으로 게임 퍼블리셔와 콘텐츠 IP(Intellectual Property, 지식재산권) 보유 기업에게 오프라인 공간은 디지털 콘텐츠를 현실로 가져오는 중요한 접점이다. 엔씨는 도쿄게임쇼에서 85형과 32형 스페이셜 사이니지를 부스 입구와 대기 공간 등에 배치해 관람객이 이동하는 과정에서도 게임 속 캐릭터와 세계관을 자연스럽게 경험하도록 했다. 부스 입구에는 85형 스페이셜 사이니지로 ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 게임의 주요 배경인 ‘특구청’ 건물 내 엘리베이터를 재현했다. 대형 디스플레이를 통해 캐릭터를 실제 사람과 가까운 크기로 표현해, 마치 게임 속 등장인물들이 현실 세계에 인사를 건네는 듯한 장면을 연출했다. ▲ ‘아스트라에 오라티오’ 부스 입구에 설치한 85형 스페이셜 사이니지는 게임 속 다양한 캐릭터가 눈 앞으로 다가오는 듯한 연출로 관람객의 이목을 끌었다. 엔씨 아스트라에 오라티오 사업실 이용수 실장은 “관람객들이 부스에 들어서는 순간부터 실제 크기의 캐릭터와 마주하고 게임 세계에 몰입하길 바랐다”면서 “서브컬처 장르에서는 캐릭터의 생동감과 현실감이 특히 중요한데, 스페이셜 사이니지가 이런 특성을 관람객에게 효과적으로 전달할 수 있다고 판단했다”고 말했다. 현장을 찾은 관람객들은 스페이셜 사이니지가 구현한 캐릭터의 크기와 입체감에 주목했다. 콘텐츠 크리에이터 카와이 코코(Kawaii CoCo) 씨는 “캐릭터가 실제로 움직이며 상호작용하는 것처럼 생생하게 느껴졌다”며 “일반 디스플레이보다 훨씬 눈에 띄고 소셜미디어에서도 근사하게 보일 것 같아, 이 장면을 촬영해 제 구독자들에게 소개하고 싶다”고 말했다. ▲ 콘텐츠 크리에이터 카와이 코코 씨는 캐릭터의 움직임이 스페이셜 사이니지를 통해 생동감 있게 전달되어 아스트라에 오라티오 부스로 눈길이 갔다고 말했다. 스페이셜 사이니지는 52mm 1 의 얇은 두께에도 불구하고 마치 화면 뒤에 별도의 공간이 있는 듯한 깊이감을 구현한 것이 특징이다. 이러한 경험은 대중에게 게임과 캐릭터의 첫인상을 전달하는 데도 효과적으로 활용될 수 있다. 관람객 다니엘 아세로(Daniel Acero) 씨는 “처음 봤을 때 스크린 화면인 줄 전혀 몰랐고, 투명한 설치물이라고 생각했다”면서 “마치 화면 뒤에 실제 공간이 있는 것처럼 깊이감이 느껴져서 놀라웠고, 이러한 방식으로 게임 캐릭터를 소개하면 게임에 대한 관심을 높이고 캐릭터의 개성을 효과적으로 전달할 수 있을 것”이라고 말했다. 관람객 동선과 대기 공간에는 32형 스페이셜 사이니지가 설치돼 부스 전반으로 캐릭터 경험을 확장했다. 32형 제품은 49.4mm의 얇은 두께로 좁은 공간에도 유연하게 설치가 가능해, 게임 체험을 기다리는 관람객을 대상으로 캐릭터와 세계관에 대한 몰입도를 유지했다. 관람객 토마스 포르티에(Tomas items.fullText: AI Security Is an Engineering Problem — How to Solve It at Every Layer of the Agent Stack Open research, controls across the agent stack and continuous testing help defenders build and operate more secure AI systems. September 21, 2026 by Saša Zdjelar 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! AI security is an engineering problem. That means defined security requirements, enforceable controls, named owners and evidence that protections work. As AI becomes more capable, the industry must accelerate security engineering, broaden access to defensive tools and share what works faster. Technology Changes, Security Fundamentals Endure The internet and cloud computing changed how software operates, while core security responsibilities endured: establish identity, control access, limit exposure and verify that protections work. AI agents introduce new capabilities — reasoning , using tools and adapting actions based on the data they encounter. Those capabilities require applying established principles to new operating conditions. This pace creates pressure. Organizations want the productivity benefits of AI while the practices to govern and secure these systems are still developing. Security Depends on the Full Agent Stack Applications depend on code, data, identities, services and infrastructure. Security depends on how those components work together — and AI agents extend that system . Models provide capabilities; harnesses organize context, tools and workflows; and runtime environments provide the infrastructure within which actions execute. Each part of that stack carries security responsibilities, and proper protection requires controls across each layer, as data, instructions and actions move through the system. Consider an agent updating a customer record. Say it encounters malicious instructions in an attached document and attempts to export customer data to an unauthorized destination.
